content.text: {"relation":"DIVERGENT","consensus_summary":"All three blind responses converge on a settled reading: a 'name' symbolizes the identity, essential character, authority, presence, and reputation of the person who bears it — the name stands for the person themselves, especially in the case of God's name. Complementary facets include delegated authority ('in the name of'), reputation/renown, new-name transformation, and (in Response B) covenant belonging as a listed alternative.","book_summary":"The book identifies the name as 'the covenant itself' — specifically on the model of a bride taking her husband's name: to be called by His name is to be brought into covenant, under His wing/covering (Ruth 3:9; Isa 4:1), with the garment-corners recalling the commandments. It explicitly sets this against the commonly taught view (character, authority, reputation).","consensus_core_identification":"Name = the person who bears it: their essential character, nature, identity, authority, and presence.","book_core_identification":"Name = the covenant relationship itself, entered as a bride takes a husband's name; bearing the name signifies covenantal belonging and being brought under God's protective wing.","core_relation":"CONTRADICTS","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"Passages like Isaiah 4:1 ('let us be called by thy name') and Numbers 6:27-type name-bearing texts, which consensus treats as expressions of identity/ownership by the person, are reclassified by the book as covenant-marriage transactions. Exodus 20:7 is reread from 'profaning God's character/reputation' to 'bearing the covenant name unfaithfully, like an unfaithful spouse.' Many consensus cases (name = character revealed, e.g., Ex 34:5-7; name = person's authority) fall outside the book's covenant-marriage identification.","material_contradiction":"The consensus says the name symbolizes the person (character, authority, reputation); the book says it symbolizes the relationship — the covenant itself — and explicitly frames the person-centered reading as merely the 'commonly taught' view it is departing from. A name cannot in the same sense be both the bearer's own character and the covenant bond between two parties; accepting the book's identification requires displacing the consensus's central referent.","rationale":"The book does not merely narrow or sharpen the consensus reading; it replaces the referent. Where consensus identifies the name with the person who bears it, the book identifies it with the covenant relationship entered by the one who is called by it, on the bridal model of Ruth 3:9 and Isaiah 4:1. Response B does list 'covenant ownership and belonging' as a common alternative, so the book's reading is not wholly absent from the consensus landscape (hence not NOVEL), but the book elevates that relational sense into the exclusive core identification while contrasting it against the consensus primary, which constitutes replacement rather than refinement. Extension overlaps partially (name-bearing and name-calling texts remain in scope) but is systematically reclassified from person-identity to covenant-marriage.","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"Response B explicitly lists covenant belonging ('bearing or receiving a name signifies being claimed by God and included among his people,' Numbers 6:27; Isa 43:7) as a common alternative, so one could argue the book merely promotes a recognized facet to primacy — a REFINED reordering of emphasis rather than a genuine contradiction of the consensus category. Additionally, Ruth 3:9 never mentions a name at all, weakening the printed citations' support for the bridal-name identification.","confidence":"medium"}
